zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical coverage was cross-checked against the supplied Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510 (CC BY 4.0). This is a lexical aid, not a substitute transcription; the supplied BnF scan remains the authority. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ .

lines.note: Iuauo denotes rocks or rocky ground, matching Penedia and rochedo. The damaged Portuguese word is Penedia, not Peuelia; the baseline's close ourochedo spacing is retained. This headword is anticipated by f276's catchword.
Iuatçutçuji is a flower name. The Portuguese gives no more specific identification than a flower so called, so no modern botanical name is supplied.
Iuaxi is the sardine-name, directly glossed Sardinha. The surviving tall initial is capital I, not the draft's lowercase i.
Iuo and vuo are alternatives for fish. The printed initial i/u-v variation is retained; Latin l separates alternatives and is not part of either Japanese form.
This homophonous Iuo is equated with Iuori, a poor hut. The last Portuguese word is complete como, not the draft's com-, and continues with the hut comparison below.
Choupana completes the comparison, a humble hut. The short indented row belongs to the dwelling entry, not to the following sulphur entry.
Iuǒ is sulphur, glossed Enxofre. Its caron distinguishes the printed form from the unaccented Iuo entries above; the word is not modernized.

Ixa is a physician. The enlarged initial I spans this row and the following one, and the adjoining X is uppercase; OCR omitted the initial and mistook its continuation on the next row for a paragraph mark.
Ixei denotes pomp or splendour and power. There is no printed pilcrow before it: the stroke at the left is the lower part of the enlarged I assigned to IXa above.
Ixe monogatari is described as books of songs or verses. The initial I is capital; the title is ordinary Japanese entry text, not an embedded Portuguese font-toggle term.
Verßos completes the songs-or-verses description. The printed double-s-like sort is retained using the draft's ß convention rather than modernizing the spelling.

Ixeno vofarai names the small boxes pilgrims bring back from Ixe. Second-pass enlargement supports f in vofarai (not the provisional long ſ); its crossing stroke and the purification/pilgrimage context agree. The description continues through the next two rows.

runs.text: os romeiros que là vão a viſitar

lines.note: The boxes are brought from the province of Ixe by pilgrims who go there to visit the deity. Ixe is visibly upright within the italic Portuguese clause, and this continuation has the same indentation as the rows around it.
O Cami completes the pilgrims' object of worship. Cami is a Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese explanation; the local italic setting is retained.

runs.text: Sebe groſſa, ou marachão que ſe faz

lines.note: Ixeqi is a substantial barrier or embankment. The headword begins with I, not OCR D; the location and purpose of the structure are supplied below.

runs.text: ao lõgo do rio pera não leuar à terra dos cãpos.

lines.note: The embankment runs along a river to prevent the fields' earth from being carried away. The marked vowel in lõgo is o, not the draft's a; cãpos retains its nasal abbreviation.
Ixi is a physician, paraphrased by Cuſuxi. This medical homophone must remain distinct from the stone noun immediately below.
Ixi is stone. The damaged initial belongs to Ixi, not OCR Axi, and introduces the sequence of stone-related compounds.
Ixibachi denotes a stone bowl or basin. Both Bacio and bacia are retained as the two printed Portuguese alternatives.
Ixibai is lime made from stone. Initial capital I is restored; the close feitade spelling is retained instead of supplying a modern word space without secure visual grounds.
Ixibaxi is a bridge of stone. The Japanese baxi element corresponds to the Portuguese ponte, and no additional construction detail is implied.
Ixibaxira is a stone column or pillar. Columna is the historical Portuguese form and is not modernized.
Ixibiya is a cannon or other artillery piece. The scan includes the internal i missing from Ixbiya; the historical fused dartelharia is retained.

Ixibotoqe is a stone Buddhist image. The embedded Fotoque is read with a worn, open o; enlargement does not securely support the OCR's e. This damaged-vowel choice is retained as a nonblocking caveat.

runs.text: Epitaphio de letras eſculpidas em pe

lines.note: Ixibumi is a stone inscription or epitaph. The Portuguese final pe continues as pedra on the next row without a supplied hyphen.

runs.text: dra que algum defũcto deixa pera ſua memoria.

lines.note: Dra completes pedra. The inscription is left as a memorial to a deceased person; memoria, not OCR memaria, is supported by the printed rounded o.
Ixibune is a stone trough or basin, glossed Pia de pedra. The stone-vessel meaning is stated directly without interpreting the compound literally as a boat.
Ixibuxi and iximochi name a river fish. Latin l introduces the alternative, and q̃ starts the relative clause describing its habitat below.
The fish moves or lives beneath stones. The physical phrase de baixo remains separate rather than being modernized into a single word.
Ixicunangui is identified as a bird of that name. The gloss reads aßi, including the missing double-s-like sort, rather than the OCR's ai; no species identification is inferred.
Ixidacana describes a stony place or road. Its adjectival ending is confirmed by the following example modifying michi, a road.
Ixidacana michi is a rough, stony road. The Portuguese noun is Caminho, not OCR Caminhe; the second adjective continues below.
Pedregoſo completes the rough-and-stony road description. This continuation is not a separate Portuguese-only entry.

Ixidacani is the adverbial counterpart of Ixidacana, explicitly labelled Adu. The n before final i is damaged: the faint descending trace after its arch supports n rather than the draft r. The supplied NINJAL lexical index prompted this enlarged recheck but is not authority for the printed allograph; this adopted reading remains a nonblocking caveat.
Ixidatami denotes paving of square stones. The alternative beginning ou continues with the act of laying such paving.

runs.text: o ladrilhar com eſas pedras. ¶ Item, Cer

lines.note: The gloss adds paving with these stones, then begins a further sense at Cer / tas. Printed eſas is retained without supplying an expected second s.

runs.text: tas malhas, ou lauores, que hà nas peças de ſe

lines.note: Tas completes Certas and introduces patterns or ornamental work on silk pieces. The final ſe continues as ſeda without an inferred hyphen.

runs.text: da, esteiras, &c. à maneira de ladrilhos de

lines.note: Da completes ſeda; mats are also mentioned. The patterns are compared with ordered stone paving, with the comparison continued below.
Pedra aſſentados por ordem completes the comparison with regularly laid stone slabs. It closes the figurative decorative-pattern sense of ixidatami.
Ixidôro is a stone lantern. Initial I is capital and the existing circumflex reading over o is retained, without imposing an accent from modern pronunciation.
Ixifibachi is a stone brazier or fire container. The Portuguese Fogareiro supplies the heating function, not a general stone bowl.
Ixigame is glossed as a turtle. The entry does not provide enough detail to assert a particular modern species.
Ixigura is equated with Ixicaqi and defined as a wall. The stone material is supplied on the following row; the Japanese synonym is not a Portuguese-embedded font-toggle term.
Pedra completes the wall-of-stone definition. This short continuation closes ixigura before the unrelated adjective ixij.

runs.text: Couſa goſtoſa, ou de bom ſabor: quando

lines.note: Ixij describes something tasty or of good flavour. The scan restores initial I, feminine goſtoſa and bom; the usage qualification begins at quando and continues at the top of column 2.

runs.text: ſe vſa neſte ſentido commummente vſão molhe

lines.note: Continues the tasty/good-tasting sense of Ixij from the foot of column 1: the dictionary says that women commonly use the word in this sense. The physical line ends in molhe without a supplied hyphen; res follows on the next row.

Completes molheres, then introduces a metaphorical application, Ixû or ixicu mǒſu, saying something well or agreeably. The u of Ixû has a visible circumflex, also repeated in the short derivative below; mǒ remains physically divided from ſu.

runs.text: Dizer algũa couſa bem dita, & a gosto

lines.note: The initial ſu completes mǒſu, the Japanese verb of saying on the preceding row. The Portuguese describes saying something well expressed and to the liking of the hearers; the final phrase continues with de todos.
The two-word continuation de todos completes the explanation: the remark pleases everyone, not just the speaker. It belongs to the metaphorical use of Ixij, not to the following new verb.

Ixiſa is the bare nominal derivative of the preceding adjective, its quality or degree of pleasantness/tastiness. The scan gives only the Japanese form and a period, so no gloss is supplied in the transcription.
Ixû is the corresponding adverbial form of the preceding adjective. This independent short row repeats the circumflex-bearing form seen in the metaphorical example, not the grave-accented OCR Ixù.

Ixiramacaxi gives a verb paradigm for bringing down or making people retreat under fire, as the next row explains. The scan supports capital I, continuous Abater, and fazer ending in r; the OCR division A bater and final s are not retained.

runs.text: retirar a gente às frechadas, ou eſpingardadas.

lines.note: Completes the action: drive people back with arrow shots or firearm shots. Enlargement shows a small grave accent over the a of às; frechadas is the printed historical spelling, not modernized to flechadas.
Ixiſotoba is a stone grave marker. The Portuguese begins with a stone erected on the deceased person’s grave; the initial capital I is visible, and the inscription is described on the next row.
Completes the grave-marker definition: the stone stands on the grave of the deceased and bears some writing. Defunto is printed here without the c found in other historical spellings on this page.

Ixitataqi is identified by the Portuguese bird name Alueloa, followed by paſſaro. This is a bird entry, distinct from the adjoining stone objects; the older Portuguese name is retained rather than replaced by a modern zoological label.
Ixitçuigi denotes a stone wall. The capital initial and the printed tçui sequence are retained; the headword is not reshaped to a modern Japanese spelling.

Ixiuchino ſoya names a particular kind of arrow. Certa laya is the Portuguese classification formula “a certain kind”; the Japanese expression occupies the headword position, not an embedded Portuguese term.
Ixiuſu is a stone mill or millstone, rendered Mò depedra. The grave accent and the closely joined depedra are retained from the aligned reading; they are not silently modernized to mó de pedra.

runs.text: Gral de pedra em que moem me-

lines.note: Ixiyaguen is a stone mortar in which medicines are ground. The word mezinhas is physically divided after me-; this is a pharmaceutical implement rather than the preceding grinding stone in general.
The short continuation zinhas completes me-zinhas, “medicines,” in the stone-mortar definition. The period closes that entry.

runs.text: Monte, ou ſerra de muitas pedras.

lines.note: Ixiyama denotes a rocky mountain or range, literally a mountain characterized by many stones. The scan shows a terminal period after pedras, which was absent from the draft.

runs.text: Feição de crista de galo baixa, &

lines.note: Ixizaca describes a particular shape of cock’s comb: low, with the second dimension supplied on the next row. The printed Portuguese crista and the Japanese zaca are preserved rather than regularized.
Larga completes the cock’s-comb description: the comb is low and broad. This is not an independent adjective entry.
Ixizaxi is equated with Ixicaqi, then defined as a wall or enclosure of stone. The marker i, introduces a Japanese synonym, so Ixicaqi is not an embedded Portuguese typeface term.
Pedra completes both alternatives in the preceding gloss: a stone wall or stone enclosure. The row contains only this continuation and the closing period.
Ixizuye denotes foundation stones. The Portuguese starts describing stones placed underneath timber buildings; the spatial phrase de baixo continues across the row break.
Completes the description of foundation stones beneath wooden buildings, then begins the example Ixizu-yeno iye. The terminal hyphen belongs to the Japanese word, not to the Portuguese definition.
Yeno iye completes Ixizuyeno iye, a house founded on these stones. The explanatory Portuguese says exactly that; the Japanese example stays in its original two-row physical arrangement.

The two Japanese expressions mean to set the foundation stones, or to set stones in place. The Portuguese gloss begins with A- and continues on the next physical row; the printed vel marker l, is not modernized.
Completes A-ſentar: to lay or set the stones of the building. Only one long ſ is printed at this row’s beginning; no additional s is inserted to regularize the verb.

runs.text: Ferro que põẽ no cabo dos bordoẽs,

lines.note: Ixizzuqi is the iron fitting at the end of a staff, spear, or similar object. The scan reads Ferro, with rr rather than the OCR tr; the supplied nasal spellings põẽ and bordoẽs remain unchanged.
Adds spears and other objects to the examples of shafts fitted with the iron end-piece. The printed &c. closes the list.
Ixǒ is glossed simply as clothing or a garment. The mark over o opens upward like a caron, in contrast to the following homographic-looking entry’s circumflex.

Ixô is paraphrased by Nocoxi teraſu and concerns the good example left by a person’s life. The scan has a circumflex over o, unlike Ixǒ immediately above; the explanation continues with the person’s death.

runs.text: que hum deixou depois de morto.

lines.note: Completes the moral-example sense: the good example a person left after death. It does not extend the earlier clothing sense.

Ixocu is explained by Qirumono, cuimono, things to wear and things to eat. The Portuguese begins with clothing and joins the following comer; the Japanese pair is a headword paraphrase, not an embedded Portuguese phrase.
Comer completes the paired definition of Ixocu: clothing and food/eating. It is a one-word continuation, not a separate dictionary entry.
Ixu, paraphrased as Cocorono vomomuqi, denotes one’s view, inclination, or opinion. The second Portuguese synonym continues on the next line.
Completes opinião and introduces Ixuuo mǒxi ſanzuru, expressing what is in one’s mind. The Portuguese begins De-, whose remaining letters are on the next row.

runs.text: ſabafar dizẽdo o q̃ tenho no coração, ou cuido.

lines.note: Completes De-ſabafar, to unburden oneself by saying what is in one’s heart or what one thinks. Enlarged comparison shows ſabafar, including the a before b; the OCR Ciafar loses several letters and does not fit the printed verb. The abbreviations dizẽdo and q̃ are retained.
Ixǔ, paraphrased as Coromono ſode, means the sleeves of a garment. The caron over u distinguishes this headword from unaccented Ixu above; the Portuguese vestido retains the baseline s form.
Ixxa is paraphrased as Fitotçuno iſago and defined as a single grain of sand. This literal minimum supplies the figurative extension on the next row.
The additional sense is “a very small amount/thing,” extending the image of a single grain of sand. Item marks this as a further use of Ixxa, not a new headword.
Ixxe, Fitotçuno yo, denotes an entire lifetime. The alternative Portuguese formulation “while one lives” begins here and continues below.
Quanto hum viue completes em quanto hum viue, the duration for which someone lives. This closes the lifetime definition of Ixxe.
Ixxeno aida is declared Idem: the same lifetime or whole-life duration as Ixxe. The added Japanese aida expresses the interval.
Ixxecai denotes the whole world. The Portuguese gloss is complete on this row and should not be joined to the following battle entry.
This Ixxen means one battle. Although the initial I is faint, its upright trace is present at the left of xxen; it is restored rather than treating the headword as initial-less.
A separate Ixxen, paraphrased as Fitotçuno itoſugi, means one thread of silk. The repeated spelling is intentional homophony, not a duplicated battle entry.
Ixxeqi is paraphrased as a single evening and glossed Hũa tarde. The initial of tarde is an italic t, not capital I; the caron in yǔbe is preserved.

This second Ixxeqi concerns all movable and landed property, not an evening. Both x letters and the i in Fitotçuno are visible. The definition continues at the top of f278; the separate bottom catchword previews that continuation and is not part of this body row.
